summary: Describes how to advertise generic application information, meaning data not directly related to IS-IS operation itself, in IS-IS link state packets. It also gives guidelines for flooding that information so it does not harm routing.

plainLanguage.summary: A town crier mostly announces road news, but sometimes carries other notes too. This sets the rules so the extra notes do not drown out the road news.

questions: how to advertise application data in is-is
can is-is carry non routing information
what is the is-is geninfo tlv
what is an is-is application id
subtitle: A single IS-IS TLV that carries any application's data without using up the protocol's limited type codes.

tldr.problem: IS-IS has only 256 TLV type codes, and carrying more non-routing application data in link state packets could use up many of them and could disturb routing.
tldr.mechanism: A single Generic Information (GENINFO) TLV, type 251, holds flags, a 16-bit Application ID and application-specific data, with flooding rules and a requirement to use a non-zero IS-IS instance.
tldr.outcome: Applications can share one TLV codepoint, scoped by a registered Application ID, while the rules limit harm to routing.

today: RFC 6823 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2012. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Generic TLV
sections.content:
IS-IS sends information in TLVs (Type-Length-Values). The type is one octet, so only 256 codepoints exist. That has been generous for the protocol's own needs, but advertising generic information (GENINFO) that is not directly related to IS-IS operation could consume many of them.

RFC 6823 defines an encoding that uses few TLV codepoints and leaves the format of the information flexible. It also describes good behavior when advertising and flooding LSPs that contain GENINFO, so that stale information is avoided and duplicate or conflicting information is minimized. How the information passes between IS-IS and the application is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only so many kinds of announcement cards. One flexible card for everyone's extra notes keeps the supply from running out.

sections.title: The GENINFO TLV
sections.content:
The GENINFO TLV has type 251, and its length is the number of octets in the value (3 to 255). The value holds a 1-octet Flags field, a 2-octet Application ID, 0 to 20 octets of application IP address info, and then additional application-specific information.

The Flags are S (0x01), D (0x02), I (0x04) and V (0x08). If I is set, a 4-octet IPv4 address follows the Application ID. If V is set, a 16-octet IPv6 address follows the Application ID, or follows the IPv4 address when I is also set. These addresses are not necessarily those of a router running IS-IS.

Application IDs are unsigned 16-bit numbers from 1 to 65535, assigned through an IANA registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The card has a few check boxes, a number saying which group owns it, optional addresses, and then room for the group's own message.

sections.title: Sub-TLVs for Applications
sections.content:
A GENINFO TLV MAY carry sub-TLVs in its application-specific part, as introduced by RFC 5305. Receivers are required to ignore sub-TLVs they do not understand, so new information can be added in a backwards compatible way.

Their codepoints are scoped by the GENINFO TLV codepoint together with the Application ID, so they are private to the application. They are called APPsub-TLVs, are unsigned 8-bit numbers (0 to 255), and their management is outside this document. Nested sub-TLVs use a one-octet Type, a one-octet Length and zero or more octets of Value.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group can put smaller labeled notes inside its card, and its labels mean something only for that group. Readers skip notes they do not know.

sections.title: Flooding and Leaking Rules
sections.content:
Each GENINFO TLV describes exactly one application instance. If information with the same Application ID needs different flooding scopes, a router MUST originate at least one TLV per scope. With the S bit clear the TLV has area or level scope and MUST NOT be leaked into another level. With S set it has domain scope and MUST be leaked into other levels.

When a TLV is leaked from Level-2 to Level-1, the D bit MUST be set, and TLVs with D set MUST NOT be leaked from Level-1 to Level-2, which prevents looping. A router leaking downward MUST compare TLV contents so that its LSPs for a level never hold two copies of the same GENINFO TLV.

A system MUST NOT use, or leak, a GENINFO TLV from a system that is not currently reachable at that level, to avoid stale data after an area partition. Updates SHOULD go in the LSP with the same number as the one they replace, or the two LSPs SHOULD be flooded atomically. Receivers MAY use a hold-down time, and non-conflicting attributes in two TLVs with the same Application ID are additive. For conflicts, the choice is undefined.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say how far a note may travel, stop notes from going in circles, and make sure nobody keeps passing along an old note after the sender is cut off.

sections.title: Use a Separate Protocol Instance
sections.content:
Flooding non-routing data through IS-IS degrades the protocol, because LSP updates become more frequent and routers spend resources processing the data. So GENINFO advertisement MUST occur in a non-zero instance of IS-IS as defined in RFC 6822, unless use in the zero instance is defined in a Standards Track RFC.

A separate instance still calls for care: changes should be dampened to avoid flooding storms, and documents using GENINFO MUST define the expected rate of change. Separate non-zero instances can give independent flooding scope control to different applications. GENINFO MUST NOT alter basic IS-IS operation, including adjacencies, the update process and the decision process.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing news should not wait behind other notes, so the extra notes ride on their own separate announcer.

sections.title: Rules for Applications
sections.content: GENINFO is meant for applications whose operation is defined in a public specification. That specification MUST include a description of the sub-TLV allocation policy, a discussion of security issues, a discussion of the rate of change of the advertised information, and a justification for using GENINFO.
sections.plainLanguage: A group must write down its plan in public, including how its labels work and why it needs the card, before using it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Security
sections.content:
IANA registered TLV type 251, Generic Information, valid in LSPs only. IANA also created a registry of Application Identifiers, 1 to 65535, with 0 reserved. The procedure is Expert Review, and the expert MUST verify that the public specification covers the points in Section 7. Each entry records the ID value, description, whether it is allowed in instance zero, and the reference specification.

The new TLV raises no new IS-IS security issues by itself, but an application's data might. The application's specification MUST discuss them, and use of RFC 5304 or RFC 5310 authentication is recommended where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of the list hands out the group numbers and checks each group wrote its plan. Groups must also think about safety, and authentication is a good idea.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved bits plus V, I, D and S flags.

fields.name: Application ID
fields.desc: Identifier assigned through the IANA registry.

items.label: S
items.desc: Set: flood across the whole domain. Clear: do not leak between levels.

items.label: D
items.desc: Set when leaked from Level-2 to Level-1; prevents looping.

items.label: I
items.desc: A 4-octet IPv4 address follows the Application ID.

items.label: V
items.desc: A 16-octet IPv6 address follows the Application ID or IPv4 address.
